title: Ames: five concurrents — faith properly in pious affection, rest, and apprehension
source_text: XXXI. Amesius autem sic ea de re Philosophatur: Ad fidem divinam, inquit, quinque ista concurrunt: 1. Notitia rei a Deo testatae; 2. Affectio pia erga Deum, quae facit ut maxime valeat apud nos ipsius testimonium; 3. Assensus qui praebetur veritati testatae, propter hanc affectionem erga Deum, ejus est ejus testis; 4. Acquiescentia in Deum ad illud quod proponitur consequendum; 5. Electio vel apprehensio rei ipsius, quae in testimonio nobis exhibetur. Primum, nempe, notitia ex ejus mente, ad fidem requiritur, sed illam non constituit. Tertium, scilicet, assensum vult esse effectum fidei. Adeoque docet fidem proprie consistere in tribus reliquis, videlicet in pia illa affectione, acquiescentia in Deum, & apprehensione boni, quod nobis in Verbo Dei proponitur. In Medulla Theologiae lib. 1. cap. 3.
pass_a_gloss: But Ames philosophizes thus about the matter: To divine faith, he says, these five concur: 1. Knowledge of the thing attested by God; 2. A pious affection toward God, which makes His testimony weigh most with us; 3. Assent which is given to the attested truth, because of this affection toward God, whose is His witness; 4. Resting in God unto obtaining that which is proposed; 5. Choice or apprehension of the thing itself which is exhibited to us in the testimony. The first, namely knowledge, on his mind is required for faith, but does not constitute it. The third, namely assent, he will have to be an effect of faith. And so he teaches that faith properly consists in the three remaining — namely in that pious affection, resting in God, and apprehension of the good which is proposed to us in the Word of God. In the Marrow of Theology, book 1, chapter 3.
pass_b_english: Ames: five things concur in divine faith.
Knowledge of what God attests; pious affection toward God; assent; rest in God; choice/apprehension of the good shown.
Knowledge required but does not constitute faith; assent is an effect.
Faith properly = pious affection + rest in God + apprehension of the proposed good.
